strategies.name: Long Call
strategies.description: Buy a call: unlimited upside with premium at risk. The purest bullish expression with a convex payoff and no liquidation risk.
strategies.whatIs: The most fundamental bullish option trade: you pay a premium upfront for the right — not the obligation — to buy the underlying at a fixed strike. Your downside is capped at that premium while your upside is mathematically unlimited, producing the classic convex 'hockey stick' payoff.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you expect a strong directional move higher within the option's lifetime, when implied volatility is low or rising, and when you want defined risk without liquidation mechanics. It suits catalysts such as protocol upgrades, ETF flows or macro prints where a large up-move is plausible but not guaranteed.
advantages: Defined risk — the maximum loss is exactly the premium paid, known before entry
Unlimited profit potential with payoff convexity that accelerates as spot rallies
No margin or liquidation engine — unlike perps, an adverse move cannot force-close you
Cheap leverage: a small premium controls a much larger notional exposure
Positive gamma — the position grows stronger in your favor and weaker against you
disadvantages: Theta bleed: the premium decays every day, accelerating into expiry
Needs a move large enough to overcome the premium before breakeven is reached
A volatility crush after an event can lose money even when direction is right
100% loss of premium is common on quiet or slowly-grinding markets
Long-dated calls sacrifice most of their extrinsic value if held to expiry while OTM
strategies.mechanics: You buy one call at (typically) at-the-money strike. Its value splits into intrinsic value (spot above strike) and extrinsic value (time + volatility). As spot rises the delta climbs from ~0.5 toward 1, so each further dollar up adds nearly a full dollar of P&L per contract — that is positive gamma at work. Time works against you: theta drains the extrinsic portion daily, with roughly a third of the time value decaying in the final weeks. Vega is strongly positive, so rising implied volatility can rescue a stagnating position, while a post-event IV crush punishes it. Profit at expiry = max(spot − strike, 0) − premium; breakeven sits at strike + premium. Manage it by rolling up/out to capture gains, or by taking profit when delta approaches 1 and convexity is exhausted. strategies.name: Deep ITM Call (Stock Replacement)
strategies.description: High-delta deep-in-the-money call replicates spot with far less capital at risk and no liquidation engine.
strategies.whatIs: A call struck far below spot (typically 0.75–0.85× spot) with delta near 0.9–1.0. It behaves like a leveraged, fully-collateralized long position in the underlying — 'stock replacement' — because almost all of its value is intrinsic.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you want long exposure that tracks spot nearly 1:1 but with strictly limited downside and no liquidation engine, typically for multi-week swings or when you want to avoid parking full notional in spot. Also used to park capital efficiently while preserving convexity in case of a violent rally.
advantages: Near-1.0 delta gives spot-like exposure for a fraction of the notional capital
Maximum loss is still bounded at the (mostly intrinsic) premium
Tiny extrinsic value means theta bleed is negligible
No funding payments and no liquidation risk like a perpetual future
Retains a sliver of convexity if spot explodes higher
disadvantages: Large capital outlay relative to ATM/OTM calls — leverage is modest
Intrinsic value moves 1:1 down as well as up — no cushion on the downside
Opportunity cost if the market goes nowhere — you earn no yield on the structure
Thinner convexity: gamma is minimal, so no payoff acceleration
Liquidity on deep strikes can be poorer with wider spreads
strategies.mechanics: The call trades close to spot − strike (its intrinsic value) plus a small time premium. Delta ≈ 1 means it moves like the underlying; gamma ≈ 0 means the exposure does not accelerate. Because extrinsic value is small, theta and vega are nearly irrelevant — this is directional exposure, not a volatility trade. If spot falls below the deep strike you retain only the residual option value, capping the disaster relative to owning spot outright. Traders often finance the position by selling an OTM call against it, turning it into a deep-ITM bull call spread ('poor man's covered call') to harvest some carry. strategies.name: Bull Call Spread
strategies.description: Buy ATM call, sell OTM call: cheaper bullish exposure with capped upside and far lower theta bleed.
strategies.whatIs: A vertical debit spread: buy a call at a lower strike and sell a call at a higher strike, same expiry. You pay a smaller net debit for bullish exposure, financing part of the long call by giving away the upside beyond the short strike.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you expect a moderate, defined rally — enough to reach the short strike but not a parabolic move. Ideal when IV is elevated (the short leg subsidizes the long) or when you want to dampen theta bleed on a directional call purchase.
advantages: Cheaper than an outright call — lower premium at risk and lower breakeven
Theta bleed is materially reduced by the short call's decay
Short strike offsets vega, muting damage from a volatility crush
Max profit, max loss and breakeven are all known exactly at entry
Higher probability of profit than an OTM long call for the same thesis
disadvantages: Upside is hard-capped at the short strike — a moonshot leaves money on the table
Still loses the entire net debit if the market stalls or falls
Negative gamma near the short strike as expiry approaches
Early wind-down can be costly if the spread goes deep ITM and liquidity thins
Assignment/pin risk around the short strike at expiry
strategies.mechanics: The spread's value equals long-call value minus short-call value. Net debit = premium paid − premium received. At expiry: max profit = (short strike − long strike) − net debit, achieved when spot finishes above the short strike; max loss = net debit below the long strike; breakeven = long strike + net debit. The structure is delta-positive but vega-light — it isolates direction while stripping most of the volatility exposure. As expiry nears and spot sits between strikes, the position pins toward its binary outcome with increasing gamma. Exits are best taken with time remaining, since a fully-priced spread captures the maximum without expiry pin risk. strategies.name: Bull Put Spread (Credit)
strategies.description: Sell OTM put, buy further OTM put. Collects credit; profits if the market holds or rises. Defined tail risk.
strategies.whatIs: A vertical credit spread with a bullish-to-neutral posture: sell a put at a higher strike and buy a further-OTM put at a lower strike. You collect a net credit that you keep if the market holds above the short strike, with the long put bounding the tail.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you expect the market to rise, hold, or at worst not break the short strike — classic 'sell the dip' income. Works best in range-bound or grinding-up regimes with elevated put skew, and around levels of perceived technical support.
advantages: Collects credit upfront — profitable even if the market goes nowhere
Benefits from time decay on the short put (positive theta)
Benefits from volatility cooling off (short vega) after fear spikes
Tail risk strictly limited to strike width minus credit — no unlimited short-put exposure
Higher win-rate structure; the market has three of four directional outcomes in its favor
disadvantages: Reward is capped at the credit while the max loss is typically several times larger
Bearish break below the long strike realizes the full width loss
A volatility spike marks the position against you even if spot recovers later
Negative gamma: the position's delta grows against you as spot falls
Margin is required for a short-put structure, tying up capital
strategies.mechanics: You sell the richer (closer-to-money, more skewed) put and buy the cheaper disaster put. The credit is your max profit if spot finishes above the short strike at expiry. Max loss = (short strike − long strike) − credit, realized below the long put. Breakeven = short strike − credit. The trade is short vega and long theta — it wants calm. As spot approaches the short strike, gamma turns the delta sharply negative, which is why disciplined traders exit at a defined loss level (e.g. 2× credit) rather than riding to expiry. Rolls: if challenged, the spread can be rolled down and out in time to collect fresh credit while maintaining the thesis. strategies.name: Poor Man's Covered Call
strategies.description: Long-dated deep ITM call financed by short near-dated OTM calls: covered-call economics at a fraction of the capital.
strategies.whatIs: The Poor Man's Covered Call: a deep ITM long-dated call (the 'stock replacement') paired with a short-dated OTM call. It replicates a covered call's premium harvesting for a fraction of the capital.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you want covered-call income without owning the underlying outright, when you are moderately bullish over weeks/months, and when the long-dated deep call is available cheap relative to its intrinsic content. Best in mildly trending or range-bound markets.
advantages: Capital-efficient covered-call replication — deep ITM long leg costs far less than spot
Defined maximum loss: the debit paid for the long-dated call (minus calls collected)
Positive theta from the short near-dated call against minimal theta on the deep leg
No liquidation risk and no perp funding costs
Repeatable income: the short call can be re-sold every expiry cycle
disadvantages: Upside above the short call is capped each cycle
A crash below the deep strike realizes the full long-call debit despite income collected
Diagonal carry is sensitive to IV: a vol spike reprices future short calls richer only after it cools
Requires care matching expiries so the short never sits inside the long's final weeks
Spread costs and wide markets on deep strikes erode edge in size
strategies.mechanics: The deep ITM long call (delta ≈ 0.8–0.9, months to expiry) supplies the directional exposure; its small extrinsic value means negligible decay. Each cycle you sell an OTM call against it, collecting premium that is mostly time value. Your effective breakeven is the long-call debit minus the credits harvested. If spot rallies through the short strike, the short caps that cycle's gain — you close it (buying back near intrinsic value) and re-sell higher next cycle. The structure is a diagonal: long far-dated/low-strike, short near-dated/high-strike. Its risk is concentrated in gap risk through the long strike; the income engine keeps working as long as the long call retains intrinsic value. strategies.name: ZEBRA (Zero-Extrinsic Back Ratio)
strategies.description: Buy two ITM calls, sell one ATM call: ~100 delta stock replica with near-zero extrinsic value at entry.
strategies.whatIs: The Zero Extrinsic Back Ratio (ZEBRA): buy two ATM calls and sell one deep ITM call so the sold premium cancels the extrinsic value of the bought calls. Net extrinsic ≈ 0 gives ~100-delta stock replacement for a fraction of the capital, with no time decay.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you want synthetic long exposure without theta bleed and without paying time premium — a capital-efficient stock-replacement for swing trades. Best when you are directionally confident, expect the move within weeks, and IV is mid-range so the deep ITM short is rich in intrinsic but thin in extrinsic.
advantages: Near-zero extrinsic value: essentially no theta decay on the structure
Delivers ~0.9–1.0 delta — stock-like upside participation
Far cheaper than buying spot outright; max loss bounded at net debit
No funding payments or liquidation engine, unlike a perp long
Defined-risk long exposure that survives slow, delayed thesis realization
disadvantages: Requires a gap up to participate fully — the deep short call caps early gains below its strike
Loses the full net debit if the market collapses
Vega-light: you get almost no volatility upside on a fear rally
Three legs with strikes that must be positioned carefully at entry
Exits near expiry concentrate pin risk around the short strike
strategies.mechanics: Buy 2 ATM calls (each ~0.5 delta, extrinsic-rich) and sell 1 deep ITM call (~1.0 delta, extrinsic-poor). The combined position behaves like ~1.0 delta of stock: below the deep strike the short call goes delta-1 and neutralizes one long, leaving one long call of convexity; above ATM both longs engage. Practical management: hold the swing, exit on thesis completion; because theta ≈ 0 there is no decay pressure to force early exits. strategies.name: Call Ratio Spread 1x2
strategies.description: Sell one ATM call, buy two OTM calls: cheap or free bullish structure with doubled upside beyond the wing.
strategies.whatIs: A ratio call spread: buy 1 call at a lower strike and sell 2 calls at a higher strike, same expiry, usually for a small credit or zero cost. You get a cheap or free bullish spread whose upside flips short beyond the second short call.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you expect a moderate rally to a target level but consider a parabolic move unlikely — the market landing in the 'sweet spot' between the strikes. Often deployed around known resistance or into events where you sell the inflated upper tail.
advantages: Can be entered at zero cost or a credit — no premium at risk below the short strikes
Full profit in the moderate-rally sweet spot
Short upper strikes monetize the overpriced upside tail / call skew
Positive theta from the two short calls
A credit entry profits even if the market does nothing
disadvantages: Upside beyond the upper breakeven is naked short — unlimited loss potential
The short calls' negative gamma compounds violently in a squeeze
Wrong in a slow grind down if entered for a debit
Margin requirements are elevated due to the uncovered extra short call
Worse payoff in exactly the scenario retail buys calls for: a moonshot
strategies.mechanics: The 1×2 pays nothing (or collects) at entry. Between the long and short strikes the position is a simple bull call spread; above the short strike, the second short call turns net delta negative, and past the upper breakeven the position loses money 1:1 with every further rally. Max profit = strike width + credit at exactly the short strike at expiry. The structure is short skew and short the upper tail: it implicitly bets the market will not trade far beyond the short strike. Traders cap the disaster with a far OTM call (turning it into a call butterfly with a wide top wing) or exit on momentum breaks above the short strike. strategies.name: Call Backspread
strategies.description: Sell ITM call, buy two OTM calls: often entered for even or credit, with unlimited profit on a strong rally.
strategies.whatIs: A backspread sells 1 lower call and buys 2 higher calls, typically for a credit. It profits big from a violent rally or a sell-off (if entered at credit), while losing only in the 'dead zone' around the short strike at expiry.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you expect a large move higher — especially a potential squeeze — but want the position to at least break even (or profit) if the market drops instead. The classic use is buying upside convexity into catalysts while the credit pays you to wait.
advantages: Profits from either a strong rally or (if credit-financed) a decline
Unlimited upside above the upper breakeven with long gamma
Credit entry removes premium risk in the downside scenario
Wins exactly in the high-movement scenarios where plain long calls fail
Positive gamma — the position adds delta as the market moves your way
disadvantages: The dead zone: expiring near the short strike realizes the maximum loss
Requires a big move — moderate rallies still lose
Vega exposure is long the wings; stagnant IV with time passing bleeds value
Two long calls cost carry if the rally is slow
Strike placement is unforgiving — the sweet spot is narrow

Above the upper breakeven, the two long calls overtake the short and P&L grows unbounded — the payoff is a 'V' through the profit zone. strategies.name: Bull Call Ladder

strategies.whatIs: A bull call spread with an extra short call above: buy 1 call, sell 1 middle call, sell 1 higher call. The extra short finances the spread but caps the upside and flips the structure short above the top strike.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you expect a rally into a target zone but are confident the market will not extend beyond the top strike — e.g. rallying into a well-tested resistance. It is a cheaper bull spread funded by selling a far strike you believe is unreachable.

strategies.name: Bullish Seagull
strategies.description: Short OTM put funds a long call spread: near zero-cost bullish structure with downside risk below the put.
strategies.whatIs: A three-leg 'gull': a bull call spread where the long call is financed by selling a further OTM put. Structured to be zero-cost: the short put funds the debit spread, leaving defined-risk bullish exposure with tail risk below the put.

strategies.name: Bullish Risk Reversal
strategies.description: Sell OTM put, buy OTM call: the classic near-zero-cost bullish structure used to express direction with skew.

strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you are bullish, when put skew is rich relative to calls (fear overpriced), and when you are willing to buy the dip at the short put's strike. Common around market bottoms when downside protection demand inflates put premiums.

strategies.name: Synthetic Long
strategies.description: Buy call, sell put at the same strike: replicates the forward with no spot outlay and clean margin treatment.
strategies.whatIs: A perfect replication of the underlying: buy an ATM call and sell an ATM put at the same strike and expiry. Put-call parity guarantees this equals a futures position — full delta, full leverage, no net optionality premium.
strategies.whenToUse: Use it when you want futures-like exposure via the options market — for margin efficiency, venue access, or when options markets are deeper than perps. Also the textbook building block for conversions, boxes and parity trades.
advantages: Exactly replicates the underlying's P&L with zero net extrinsic cost (parity)
Access to leverage without spot custody or perp funding rates
Building block for arbitrage structures (boxes, conversions)
No net theta or vega — pure directional exposure
Can be struck anywhere on the chain to shape margin profiles
disadvantages: Unlimited downside exactly like a perp — no convexity at all
Carries the risk-free financing implied by forward pricing
Two legs of spread cost versus one futures trade
Pin and expiry mechanics require rolling discipline
Exchanges may margin the legs separately, inflating capital needs
strategies.mechanics: Put-call parity: C − P = S − K·e^(−rT). The combined position's delta is ~1 (call +1, put −(−1)), gamma nets to nearly zero, vega cancels. P&L = spot − strike at expiry, identical to a forward entered at the strike-adjusted forward price. strategies.name: Long Put
